invention: a new thing or idea that someone creates
friction: the force that makes dragging things hard
farming: growing food by planting and raising animals
printing press: a machine that stamps out many copies of pages
engine: a machine that does work in place of muscle
internet: the great web that links computers across the world

chapters.title: The Idea That Started It All

pages.text: Humans are not the fastest animals, nor the strongest, nor the biggest. We have no claws, no fangs, no thick fur. And yet we, of all the creatures on Earth, have reshaped the whole planet. How? With one power no other animal has to the same degree: the power to invent. To look at a problem and dream up a tool to solve it.

image.note: An early human looking thoughtfully at a heavy rock, an idea sparking; the birth of invention

pages.text: The very first invention was fire, or rather learning to make and keep it. Fire gave warmth against the cold, light against the dark, and cooked food that was easier to eat and safer. Every invention since has followed the same simple pattern: a problem, an idea, and the courage to try something new. Let us follow a few of the greatest.

image.note: Early humans gathered round a controlled fire at night, cooking, warm; a turning point

pages.text: Picture a world with no wheels. To move anything heavy, you must drag it, and dragging is brutally hard work. Then, thousands of years ago, someone realised that a round shape rolls, and that rolling defeats the friction that makes dragging so hard. The wheel was born, and suddenly one person could move what once took many.

image.note: A heavy load being dragged with great effort, then rolling easily on a simple cart; contrast

pages.text: From that single round idea came the cart, the chariot, the water wheel that ground grain, and eventually the car, the train and the machine. Nearly everything that carries, turns or spins in your world today is a child of that first wheel. It is one idea, thousands of years old, still rolling under everything you use.

image.note: A wheel at the centre, lines radiating out to a cart, a train, a car, a turbine; one idea, many fruits

pages.text: Long ago, every person had to spend nearly all day just finding food, hunting and gathering enough to survive. Then came perhaps the greatest change of all: farming. People learned to plant seeds, raise animals, and grow their food in one place. For the first time, one farmer could feed many people.

image.note: Early farmers planting and harvesting, a village with grain stores; settled, plentiful

pages.text: This changed everything. Because not everyone had to farm, some people were free to become builders, weavers, teachers and thinkers. Farming is the invention that made towns, cities and civilisation itself possible. Every great thing humans have built since stands, in the end, on the humble idea of planting a seed and waiting.

image.note: A farm feeding a growing town of builders, weavers and scholars; the seed of civilisation

pages.text: For most of history, books had to be copied out by hand, so they were rare and dear, and only the rich could learn from them. Then, about five hundred years ago, came a machine that could stamp out pages by the hundred: the printing press. One book could suddenly become a thousand.

image.note: An early printing press churning out pages; a stack of identical books growing; abundance

pages.text: The result was a flood of knowledge. Ordinary people learned to read. Ideas spread across whole countries in months instead of centuries. The book you hold in your hands right now exists because of that machine. The printing press did not just make books cheaper. It handed knowledge to everyone, and knowledge, once shared, is very hard to take back.

image.note: Ordinary people of all kinds reading books in a market square; knowledge spreading; empowering

pages.text: For thousands of years, all work was done by muscle: human muscle, or the muscle of oxen and horses. Then, about two hundred years ago, people invented engines, machines that could do the work of hundreds of horses without ever tiring. First powered by steam, later by fuel and electricity, engines changed the world at breathtaking speed.

image.note: A powerful early steam engine driving machines in a factory; smoke, energy, a new age

pages.text: Machines could weave cloth, dig mines, pull trains and build things faster than anyone had dreamed. This was called the Industrial Revolution, and it made some places enormously rich, though often through very hard labour. For better and for worse, the age of the machine reshaped how nearly all people lived and worked.

image.note: A busy industrial city of the past, factories and trains; a mix of progress and hard toil

pages.text: For almost all of history, a message could travel no faster than a person on a horse or a ship. To send word across the world took months. Then, within a single lifetime, everything sped up. First the telephone let voices leap across wires. Then radio and television sent words and pictures through the very air.

image.note: An old telephone, a radio, a television, each sending signals; the world getting smaller

pages.text: And in your own time came the greatest leap of all: the computer and the internet, which link nearly the whole world into one great web. Now a child in Abuja can speak face to face with a friend in another country in an instant, for almost nothing. Distance, which once ruled human life completely, has been all but defeated.

image.note: A modern video call: a Nigerian child waving to a friend across the world on a tablet; connected

pages.text: Here is the most important thing to understand about all these inventions. Every single one began as a thought in an ordinary person's mind. None of them fell from the sky. Someone looked at a problem everyone else accepted, and refused to accept it, and imagined something better. That is all an inventor is.

image.note: An ordinary-looking person with a bright idea, surrounded by faint sketches of a new machine

pages.text: The world you have inherited is full of problems still waiting for their inventor. Cleaner power. Better medicine. Fairer ways to live together. Perhaps the person who solves one of them is reading this book right now. Every great invention began with a curious mind that asked a simple, powerful question: could this be done better? Now it is your turn to ask.

image.note: A Nigerian child at a desk sketching an invention, eyes bright; the next inventor; closing, hopeful
